items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: So in January of 1934, Dickie Wells and I joined Teddy at the Savoy... The other members of the band were... Leon 'Chu' Berry on tenor sax

ctx.x: The word got around very quickly and Teddy Hill asked me and Dickie Wells to join his band. Willie Bryant was an M.C. and showman who had an act with another showman named Leonard Reed, who was forming an orchestra, and he engaged Teddy Wilson, Johnny Russell, Glyn Pacque and Cozy Cole. We all hated to see this band of Benny's break up and I considered and still do consider it the best band I ever played with.

So in January of 1934, Dickie Wells and I joined Teddy at the Savoy and I was back home again. The other members of the band were Bernard Flood, who along with Dillard and myself were the trumpet section. Hoe Britton was the other trombonist. Howard Johnson and Harold Blanchard on alto saxs and Leon 'Chu' Berry on tenor sax, Sam Allen, piano, John Smith, guitar, Richard 'Dick' Fullbright, bass and Bill Geeson on drums.

The Savoy was jumping as it always did and I was happy to be back in a place where it was not necessary to stand on the back stairway or go to a band room when I finished playing a set. The girls didn't have to call me from a telephone booth and I lived five minutes walking distance from the Savoy if I decided to go straight home after the night was finished. But that happened very seldom.

items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: Sammy played piano and Chu Berry whom I had met in Wheeling, West Virginia, was the tenor man.

ctx.x: The first time I played with three trumpets was when Gus Mo Clung, whom I had first heard with Scott, came back in the orchestra. Gus had a dispute with Don Redman when Scott had been in New York long before I joined them. Gus played with Clarence Page in Cincinnati in preparation to joining the Cotton Pickers after he left Scott and when Don was engaged to lead the Cotton Pickers, the first thing he did was to fire Gus.

So Gus joined our band in Cincinnati and Lloyd let Frank Newton go when we returned to the Savoy. We were in the Savoy when Marion Hardy's Alabamians came with Cab Calloway who sang through a megaphone three feet long. Eddie Mallory, one of the trumpet players became one of the ex-husbands and Charlie 'Fat Man' Turner eventually opened a bar called 'Fat Man's' on 155th Street and St. Nicholas Avenue that became very popular. Cab took over the leadership of a band called the Missourians which eventually became his…

Fletcher Henderson was engaged for one night and we had played some numbers which I don't remember what it was, but the dancers did not want us to stop and we played for a half hour longer before we finally left the stand and when the public saw that we were not coming back,
